title: Episode 2 · The South · 13 states
regionDefinition: Remaining US Census South states after episode 1; DC is not a state
intro: Welcome to episode two. First, I clear the map. Today we explore thirteen new states in the South, without repeating episode one.
Using the Census definition, these are all the Southern states we have left to cover. We'll move through Appalachia, the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, then west.

states.name: West Virginia
states.transition: Let's begin in the Appalachian interior, where West Virginia, Kentucky and Tennessee form our first group.
lines: West Virginia is the irregular mountain state west of Virginia. It is landlocked, with Kentucky to the southwest and Ohio across the river to the northwest.
The card explains its unusual name and history: it separated from Virginia during the Civil War and became a state in 1863.
Remember West Virginia as a separate state, with a northern panhandle and an eastern one. We now move southwest into Kentucky.

states.name: Kentucky
lines: Kentucky stretches west from West Virginia, directly above Tennessee. Its winding northern edge follows the Ohio River for much of the way.
The card's name origin is uncertain, but its cave fact is clear: Mammoth Cave is the world's longest known cave system.
Picture Kentucky as the upper half of a long east-west pair. Tennessee is the lower half, and our next stop.

states.name: Tennessee
lines: Tennessee is the long, narrow state immediately south of Kentucky. It runs from the Mississippi River in the west to the Appalachian mountains in the east.
Its name comes from Tanasi, a Cherokee town. The card notes that Tennessee borders eight states, tying Missouri for the most.
Keep Kentucky above Tennessee. Below Tennessee sit Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia; east of its mountains lies North Carolina.

states.name: North Carolina
states.transition: Now move east to the Atlantic side. We'll follow North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia down the coast.
lines: North Carolina is the long state below Virginia, reaching from the mountains to the Atlantic. Notice the thin Outer Banks along its eastern coast.
Carolina comes from Carolus, the Latin form of Charles. Near Kitty Hawk, the Wright brothers made their first successful airplane flights in 1903.
For your map memory, North Carolina is the broad northern Carolina, with mountains at one end and barrier islands at the other.

states.name: South Carolina
lines: South Carolina sits below North Carolina and northeast of Georgia. Its compact shape slopes southeast toward the Atlantic.
Its card takes us to Charleston Harbor. Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter there in April 1861, beginning the Civil War.
Remember the Carolina pair: the longer North Carolina above, the smaller South Carolina below. Georgia is next to the southwest.

states.name: Georgia
lines: Georgia lies south of Tennessee and west of South Carolina. It reaches the Atlantic, while its wide southern border rests above Florida.
Its name honours King George the Second. The card also connects Georgia with Martin Luther King, Junior, who was born in Atlanta in 1929.
Think of Georgia as the broad state above Florida. Alabama is to its west; now follow the coast down onto the Florida peninsula.

states.name: Florida
states.transition: Let's frame all of Florida, including its western panhandle and the peninsula stretching south between two coasts.
lines: Florida is the long peninsula below Georgia, with a panhandle extending west toward Alabama. The Atlantic lies to its east and the Gulf to its west.
Its Spanish name means flowery. The Everglades in southern Florida are often called a river of grass: a broad, shallow, slow-moving flow of water.
Remember both parts of Florida: the south-pointing peninsula and the west-reaching panhandle. The panhandle leads us toward Alabama.

states.name: Alabama
states.transition: We'll move west along the Gulf Coast, studying Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana as a connected group.
lines: Alabama sits west of Georgia and south of Tennessee. Its small coastal opening reaches the Gulf beside Florida's panhandle.
The card points north to Huntsville, nicknamed Rocket City. NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center there helped develop the Saturn rockets used for Apollo.
Keep this east-west sequence in mind: Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi. We move one state farther west next.

states.name: Mississippi
lines: Mississippi lies immediately west of Alabama, below Tennessee. Its western river border separates it from Arkansas and much of Louisiana.
Its name comes from an Indigenous expression meaning great river. The Mississippi Delta is closely associated with the origins and development of the blues.
Here the musical Delta means a region in northwestern Mississippi, not simply the river's mouth. Follow the river south toward Louisiana.

states.name: Louisiana
lines: Louisiana is the boot-shaped Gulf state west of Mississippi and south of Arkansas. The Mississippi River reaches the coast through its southeastern wetlands.
The name honours Louis the Fourteenth of France. The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 covered a vast territory, much larger than today's state.
Distinguish the modern state from that historic purchase. Keep Louisiana below Arkansas, with Texas along its western side.

states.name: Arkansas
states.transition: Now turn inland to Arkansas and Oklahoma. These belong to the Census South too, along with Texas, our final stop.
lines: Arkansas lies directly north of Louisiana and west of the Mississippi River. Oklahoma is its western neighbour; Missouri is above it.
The card links its name to the Quapaw people through French spelling. At Crater of Diamonds State Park, visitors can search for diamonds and keep their finds.
Remember Arkansas above Louisiana. Its final letter is silent, unlike Kansas, which is a different state farther northwest.

states.name: Oklahoma
lines: Oklahoma stretches west from Arkansas, directly above Texas. Notice its narrow panhandle pointing west between Kansas and Texas.
Its Choctaw-derived name means red people. The Sooner nickname recalls settlers who entered land before the official start of the 1889 land run.
Those land openings followed the dispossession of Native nations. For the map, remember Oklahoma above Texas, with Arkansas on its eastern side.

states.name: Texas
states.transition: Finally, let's give Texas a wider frame, from its northern panhandle to the Rio Grande and the Gulf Coast.
lines: Texas is the large state below Oklahoma and west of Louisiana. Its southern river border, the Rio Grande, separates it from Mexico.
The card traces its name to a Caddo word for friend or ally. Texas declared independence in 1836 and joined the United States in 1845.
Texas completes our thirteen new states. Its northern panhandle sits below Oklahoma's, while its southeastern edge reaches the Gulf.

recap: Our thirteen-state route began with West Virginia, Kentucky and Tennessee, then North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida.
Along the Gulf we added Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana; inland and west, Arkansas, Oklahoma and Texas. Pause and trace those four groups.
Together with episode one's three Southern states, that completes the Census South. We have now taught twenty-four distinct states, with no repeats between episodes.
